title: Krishna walks into the arena
hookLine: one Krishna, a whole arena, and everyone sees someone different
carry: the world is real; the mind adds the color
last: DESIRE HAS NO BEGINNING, BUT IT CAN END.

lines: ONE BOY WALKS INTO THE ARENA.
cards: Mathura, the day of King Kamsa's wrestling match. The whole city is packed into the arena. Then two young cowherds walk in from the gate: Krishna and his brother Balarama.
The Bhagavata Purana stops the story right there and looks at the crowd. To the wrestlers, Krishna is a thunderbolt. To the men, the finest of men.
To the women, love itself, walking. To the cowherds, their own boy. To wicked kings, the one who'll punish them.
To his parents, their child. To the yogis, the highest truth. And to Kamsa, up on his platform, he is death.

teach.b: One Krishna. A whole arena. A different Krishna in every mind.
The Bhagavata isn't a philosophy book, but it paints exactly what Patanjali argues in sutra 4.15: vastusamye chittabhedat tayor vibhaktah panthah.
The thing being the same, because the minds differ, the two go separate ways. Vastu is the real thing out there; chitta is the mind. Notice what Patanjali doesn't say.
He doesn't say Krishna is ten things, or nothing, or only a picture in each head. Krishna is really there, walking in. The difference is in the minds.
And 4.17 says how: a thing is known when the mind takes on its color. Picture a clear glass set on red cloth.

teach.h: FEAR SEES DEATH. LOVE SEES A CHILD.
teach.b: Many teachers read the arena this way: Kamsa's mind is colored by fear, so he sees death. His parents' minds are colored by love, so they see a child. Hindu schools argued about this for centuries.
Some Buddhist philosophers of the time held that objects are built by the mind, and the old commentary on these sutras answers them; later, Advaita Vedanta would speak of the world as maya.
Yoga, with its sister school Samkhya, takes a plain stand: the world is real.

teach.h: THE WORLD IS REAL; THE MIND ADDS THE COLOR.
teach.b: So the trouble was never the world. It's the coloring: the craving and the dread the mind lays on it. Yoga doesn't ask you to deny the chair or the cup or your brother.
It asks you to clean the glass. You've seen the small version. In 2015, one photo of a dress split the internet: blue and black, or white and gold.
Two siblings remember the same family dinner as a disaster and a delight. Same dress. Same dinner.

how: Classical Yoga, like Samkhya, is taught as a realist philosophy: the world of nature is real, and practice aims at freeing the mind from the coloring it takes on, not at denying the world. The Bhagavata's arena verse pictures the same idea: one Krishna, seen by each mind in its own way.

o: the mind's color laid over what it sees
a pleasant mood that comes after meditation
a real thing out there, not made up by the mind

games.q: one Krishna, many minds — tap the pairs.
p: the mind that takes on color

s: in the arena, Krishna changes shape for each person
he's one boy walking in. each crowd sees him through its own mind, just as sutra 4.15 says.
Patanjali teaches that the world is only in the mind
4.14–4.16 argue the object is real and doesn't depend on any one mind.
for Yoga, the trouble isn't the world but the mind's coloring
craving and fear color the glass. practice cleans the glass; it doesn't deny the world.

games.q: a friend says: if Kamsa saw death and Krishna's parents saw a child, then Krishna was only whatever people imagined. what would Patanjali say?
o: Krishna was really there; the minds differed, so they went separate ways.
right: nothing is there apart from the minds looking.
only one of them saw anything; the rest saw nothing at all.
games.why: 4.15: the thing is the same, the minds differ. Yoga is realist: the world is real, and the color comes from the mind.

practice: Let your eyes rest on one ordinary object near you, a cup, a chair, a plant, and notice the colors your mind lays on it: I like this, this needs washing, someone gave me this. Name each one softly and set it aside.
Then let the thing just be there, as itself.

wordCard.voice: Vastu, the real object out there. For Patanjali, the world is real; minds differ in how they are colored by it.

orig.note: Sanskrit vastu: a thing, a real object, something that exists.

carryVoice: Your line: the world is real; the mind adds the color. Kamsa saw death; his parents saw a child. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 10.43.17 (Krishna enters Kamsa's arena; the wrestlers, men, women, cowherds, kings, his parents, Kamsa and the yogis each see him differently)
Yoga Sutras 4.14, 4.16–4.17 (the object's own reality; not dependent on one mind; known through coloring)
Yoga Sutras 4.14–4.16, Vyasa's commentary (debate with idealist views)
